newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa's Winnie complains about treatment.
newsitem.headline: South Africa's Winnie complains about treatment.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela's former wife Winnie complained on Wednesday that South Africa's Truth Commission on apartheid-era crimes was more sympathetic to P.W. Botha, a former president from the last years of white rule, than to her.

The statutory Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) has said it would subpoena Madikizela-Mandela, as she is now known, to answer questions about the 1989 kidnapping and murder of 14-year-old activist Stompie Seipei and the disappearance of other township children.
Her lawyers Seriti, Mavundla and Partners said in a letter to the panel that she was being singled out, adding:
"It is surprising that the commission did not flex the same muscle with the former president. P.W. Botha, who displayed utter contempt for the law and the commission."

Madikizela-Mandela, 62, unsuccessfully contested President Mandela's divorce action last year. She remains a member of the highest decision-making organs of his ruling African National Congress and is elected leader of the ANC's Women's League.

Her lawyers said allegations against her should be handled with those against other members of the ANC, which has admitted a wide range of human rights violations during the 30-year struggle against apartheid.
The TRC has visited Botha, who has refused to seek amnesty for any of his actions in government, at his retirement home and has questioned him mainly in writing.

Madikizela-Mandela's driver and bodyguard was sentenced to death for murdering Seipei after he had been beaten in a room in the back yard of her Soweto home. His sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment.
Madikizela-Mandela was convicted in 1992 of kidnapping and assaulting Seipei and three other children and initially sentenced to six years in prison.
The assault charge was quashed on appeal and her sentence was reduced to a fine.

Questions have persisted about her behaviour during the final years of the war against apartheid, however, and opponents allege that new witnesses could substantiate new and more serious charges against her.
TRC investigative head Dumisa Ntsebeza said in a statement on Wednesday it would be in Madikizela-Mandela's best interest to appear before the panel and clear her name.

Quoting from a letter he wrote to her lawyers in June, he said: "Your client's name has been mentioned in the context of the murder of Stompie, in the context of the disappearance of certain youths and, we now learn, in the context of a few other matters we are investigating."
He said the allegations ranged from rumour to formal statements, but said the TRC could not ignore any form of evidence of gross human rights violation.
"We have to investigate in order to discard some rumours or information or to authenticate some information," he said.
The commission has until March next year to investigate the human rights record of the war over apartheid, to pardon offenders who willingly confess and to grant limited compensation to victims.

The deadline to apply for amnesty for human rights crimes expired on May 10, but vice chairman Alex Boraine said on Wednesday a technical extension was possible as a result of an administrative delay in passing legislation on a final deadline.
There has been no suggestion by commission or other sources that Madikizela-Mandela has applied for amnesty.
